questions.question: What is a data lakehouse?

options.text: An architecture combining data lake flexibility with data warehouse reliability and performance

questions.explanation: Data lakehouse: best of both worlds. Lake: cheap storage, any format, ML workloads. Warehouse: ACID transactions, schema enforcement, fast SQL. Technologies: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi.

questions.question: What problem does the lakehouse architecture solve?

options.text: The two-tier architecture problem—maintaining separate lake and warehouse with data duplication

questions.explanation: Traditional: data lake → ETL → data warehouse. Problems: data duplication, staleness, complexity, cost. Lakehouse: single copy of data, supports both BI and ML workloads. Simplified architecture.

questions.question: What is Delta Lake?

options.text: An open-source storage layer that brings ACID transactions to data lakes

questions.explanation: Delta Lake: Databricks open-source project. Adds to Parquet: ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, audit history. Enables lakehouse on existing data lakes. Spark integration.

questions.question: What is Apache Iceberg?

options.text: An open table format for large analytic datasets with ACID guarantees

questions.explanation: Apache Iceberg: Netflix-originated table format. Features: hidden partitioning, schema evolution, time travel, snapshot isolation. Engine-agnostic: works with Spark, Trino, Flink. Competing with Delta Lake.

questions.question: What is time travel in lakehouse context?

options.text: Ability to query historical versions of data as it existed at a specific point in time

questions.explanation: Time travel: query data at any past version. SELECT * FROM table VERSION AS OF timestamp. Use cases: audit, debugging, reproducible ML training, recovering from mistakes. Enabled by versioned metadata.

questions.question: How does lakehouse achieve ACID transactions on object storage?

options.text: Through metadata layers that track file versions and use optimistic concurrency control

questions.explanation: ACID on object storage: metadata (transaction log) tracks which files are valid. Writes create new files, update metadata atomically. Readers see consistent snapshot. No file modification—append-only.

questions.question: What is schema evolution in lakehouse?

options.text: Ability to modify table schema (add columns, change types) without rewriting data

questions.explanation: Schema evolution: add columns, rename, widen types without full rewrite. Metadata tracks schema versions. Old files read with old schema, new files with new. Backward/forward compatibility. Critical for agile data.

questions.question: What is the medallion architecture in lakehouse?

options.text: Bronze (raw), Silver (cleaned), Gold (aggregated) data layers for progressive refinement

questions.explanation: Medallion architecture: Bronze = raw ingestion, Silver = cleaned/conformed, Gold = business-level aggregates. Progressive quality improvement. Each layer is queryable. Common Databricks pattern.

questions.question: How does lakehouse support machine learning workloads?

options.text: Direct access to raw data in open formats, versioning for reproducibility, feature store integration

questions.explanation: Lakehouse ML benefits: access raw data (images, text) directly, time travel for reproducible training, feature tables with versioning, no ETL to separate ML platform. Unified analytics and ML.

questions.question: What is data compaction in lakehouse?

options.text: Combining many small files into fewer larger files for better query performance

questions.explanation: Compaction: streaming writes create many small files. Small files = slow queries (file overhead). Compaction merges into optimal-sized files. Background process. OPTIMIZE command in Delta Lake.

questions.question: Lakehouse vs traditional data warehouse: when choose warehouse?

options.text: When you need mature BI tooling, simpler operations, and primarily structured SQL workloads

questions.explanation: Choose warehouse: mature ecosystem, simpler ops, strong BI tool integration, primarily SQL users. Choose lakehouse: mixed workloads (SQL + ML), unstructured data, cost-sensitive, want single platform.

questions.question: Your company has both BI analysts using SQL and data scientists using Python/Spark. What architecture fits best?

options.text: Lakehouse—single platform supporting both SQL analytics and ML workloads

questions.explanation: Mixed workloads = lakehouse sweet spot. BI analysts: SQL on curated tables. Data scientists: Spark/Python on raw + processed data. Single source of truth. No data movement between systems.
